messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] It'd be interesting to compare Stan to this BUGS approach for binomial family, log link GLMs.
parts:
On Wednesday, May 13, 2015 at 1:17:14 PM UTC-4, Robert Grant wrote:
It is a reparameterisation in order to speed up Gibbs, though I find myself wondering "why bother". I probably will play with it at some point, though like you, my to-do list seems to stretch almost to retirement. They haven't published data, but there's nothing special about the application.

This model is not so easy to do in Stan. The Bernoulli / binomial part is pretty standard but they parameterize

log(p) = x' * beta

which requires x * beta < 1, rather than

log(p / (1 - p)) = x' * beta

which allows x * beta to be any real number.

Rejecting draws where x' * beta > 1 makes Stan draw from an invalid posterior because you can't divide by Pr(x' * beta < 1) to normalize it.

I think the way to go about it is to declare

vector<upper=1> eta;

and make the location of the prior distribution for eta[i] be (a function of) x[i]' * beta. But it is not clear how best to do that and even still it does not accomplish the authors' goals of interpreting an element of beta as a risk-ratio.

Ben

If x' is data, and we're really looking at

for fixed vector beta[1:K], then we might be able to define
a constriant on beta[K] that'd make it work if one of the x[,k]
is always negative or positive (e.g., was an intercept). A
pretty ugly function would be required to define the constraint
in terms of x and the other beta.

> which requires x * beta < 1, rather than

> log(p / (1 - p)) = x' * beta
>
> which allows x * beta to be any real number.

Is there any motivation for using a log transform rather
than logit?

>
> I think the way to go about it is to declare

> vector<upper=1> eta;

Where'd eta come from?
> But it is not clear how best to do that and even still it does not accomplish the authors' goals of interpreting an element of beta as a risk-ratio.

What's a risk ratio?

- Bob

Yes.

What's a risk ratio?

which could be obtained via posterior predictive simulations with a regular bernoulli_logit model, but I think the intended audience (medical researchers) is accustomed to only looking at ML coefficients.

messages.author: 83aa4ea66d984b54
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] It'd be interesting to compare Stan to this BUGS approach for binomial family, log link GLMs.
parts:
A big part of the motivation here is that people don't get odds ratios. Sadly, medics tend to be taught that it is an approximate risk ratio (for historical but stupid reasons) and this results in massive distortions when communicating risk to patients.

I'm also wondering if there is mileage in modelling logits as normal, including an intercept, and monitoring their corresponding risks. For continuous independent variables, you could specify a few points of interest on the scale and assess the risk at each. Or monitor the linear predictor for each observation, and then you can get marginal effects (I think; I haven't really had enough sleep to go making bold statements like that). Fundamentally, I think researchers should be giving readers risks whenever they can, and that is probably more often than ML GLMs allow.

messages.author: 3f37be0cf708d442
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] It'd be interesting to compare Stan to this BUGS approach for binomial family, log link GLMs.
parts:
one alternative way to communicate risk in an intuitively accessible way is to use average predictive comparisons:
www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/ape17.pdf
for logistic regressions they provide an estimate of by how many percentages a risk changes, if a predictor variable changes by one unit.
the one draw back of this method is that it is computationally intensive (i.e. it involves pairwise comparison of predicted outcomes for all pairs of rows in a data set), so that one has to draw a random sample of the data to compute average predictive comparisons if one has large data sets.
guido
